rules.rule: Para 13: never write, submit or commission a fake consumer review (one that purports to be, but is not, based on a person's genuine experience) or a review that conceals the fact it has been incentivised; publishing reviews in a misleading way, including by hiding negatives or giving positives greater prominence, is also covered. 'Writing' includes creating by any means, so AI-written reviews count.
Para 12: paid promotion inside editorial content must be made clear in the content or by images or sounds clearly identifiable by the consumer (advertorials, sponsored articles).
Para 7: no false claim that a product is only available for a limited time, made to elicit an immediate decision.
Para 19: no false claims that a product can prevent or treat disease, restore a physiological function, or modify a person's appearance.
Para 23: 'free', 'gratis' or 'without charge' only if the consumer pays nothing beyond the unavoidable cost of responding and of delivery.
Para 25: no posing as a consumer (for example fake grassroots posts).
Para 30: no direct appeal to children to buy, or to pester parents.
Para 3: no unauthorised trust marks. Para 14 (summarised in the harvest as fear claims about safety): read the paragraph text before writing a safety warning into an ad.

checks: Is every review or testimonial based on a genuine experience, free of fake or AI-invented reviews?
Is any incentive (free product, payment, discount) behind a review disclosed in the review?
Are negative reviews shown as readily as positive ones, with no positives given greater prominence?
Is any paid promotion inside editorial-style content clearly labelled in the content itself?
Is every 'limited time' or 'ends tonight' claim true, with a real end date?
Is 'free' used only where the consumer pays nothing beyond the unavoidable cost of responding and delivery?
Are all disease-prevention, treatment, function-restoring and appearance-changing claims true and evidenced?
Is the piece free of posing as a consumer, direct appeals to children, and unauthorised trust marks?

cards.name: W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2: success criteria that govern published copy

sources.title: W3C Recommendation 12 December 2024: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2

cards.summary: W3C Recommendation WCAG 2.2, dated 12 December 2024 (read 2026-10-04), is the current global web accessibility standard. It is a standard, not a law by itself: laws and procurement rules point to it (India's GIGW 3.0 adopts WCAG 2.1 criteria: comp:gigw_3). For writers the criteria that bite are: a text alternative for every image, captions on video, link text that says where it goes, descriptive page titles and headings, a declared page language and declared changes of language, readable text, and sufficient colour contrast.
use_for: Alt text, captions, transcripts and link text for web pages, blogs, landing pages and help centres
Page titles, headings and form labels
Bilingual Hindi-English pages (language of each passage)
Text-on-image and thumbnail copy where contrast matters
avoid: Alt text that says 'image of'. Write what the image shows or does ('Founder packing a Jaipur block-print kurta into a courier bag'). GIGW 3.0 (comp:gigw_3) gives purely decorative images a blank alt.
'Click here', 'read more' and 'learn more' as the whole link. Make the link text, or its sentence, say where it goes ('Download the GST filing checklist').
A page title like 'Home' or 'Untitled'. The page title must describe topic or purpose, and headings and labels must describe topic or purpose too.

Hindi or Hinglish blocks inside an English page with no language marking. Each passage in another language needs its language declared, except proper names, technical terms and words that have become vernacular.
Dense advanced text with no simpler version. At Level AAA, text needing more than lower-secondary reading ability should come with supplemental content or a simpler version.
Light-grey text on a photo or pastel thumbnail. Text contrast should be at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text).
applies_to: web pages, apps and video with captions

rules.rule: SC 1.1.1 (Level A): all non-text content presented to the user has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose: write alt text that says what the image shows or does, not 'image'.
SC 1.2.2 (Level A): captions are provided for all prerecorded audio content in synchronised media; SC 1.2.4 (Level AA): captions for live audio.

SC 2.4.4 (Level A): the purpose of each link can be determined from the link text alone or from the link text together with its programmatically determined link context: no bare 'click here' or 'read more'.
SC 2.4.2 (Level A): web pages have titles that describe topic or purpose; SC 2.4.6 (Level AA): headings and labels describe topic or purpose.

SC 3.1.1 (Level A): the language of the page can be programmatically determined; SC 3.1.2 (Level AA): the language of each passage can be too, except for proper names, technical terms and words that have become vernacular.
SC 3.1.5 Reading Level (Level AAA): when text requires reading ability more advanced than the lower secondary education level, supplemental content or a simpler version is provided.
SC 1.4.3 (Level AA): text contrast of at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text), which matters for text on images and thumbnails.

checks: Does every informative image have alt text that says what it shows or does, with purely decorative images given a blank alt, as GIGW 3.0 prescribes?
Do all prerecorded videos have captions (and live ones live captions where required)?
Can each link's purpose be understood from its text or its sentence?
Does the page title describe the topic, and do headings and labels describe their sections?
Is the page language declared, and is each Hindi or other-language passage marked as such (except proper names, technical terms and vernacular words)?
If the text is above lower-secondary reading level, is there a simpler version or supporting summary?
Do text and its background meet 4.5:1 contrast (3:1 for large text), including text on images and thumbnails?

cards.name: X (Twitter) Paid Partnerships Policy

sources.title: X Help Center: Paid Partnerships Policy
sources.supports: definition of paid partnership, disclosure toggle, legal compliance, prohibited industries, country rules (Australia, EU, UK)

cards.summary: X's Paid Partnerships Policy page (read in a browser 2026-10-04; the page shows no date) is the platform's own text. Creators posting paid, gifted, affiliate or ambassador content on X must switch on the 'Paid Partnership' content disclosure, follow local advertising law, and may not promote listed industries (health and wellness supplements, weight loss, pharma, alcohol, political or social-issue content and more) through paid partnerships. For India also follow comp:asci_influencer: the label goes in the post itself, not only in the platform toggle (that point is from the harvest note, not from X's page).
use_for: Sponsored, gifted, affiliate, discount-code and ambassador posts and threads on X
Influencer briefs that include an X deliverable
Deciding whether a product category can run as a paid partnership on X at all
avoid: A gifted-product post with no disclosure because 'there was no payment'. Products gifted by or on behalf of a brand count as a paid partnership.

An affiliate link or discount code with no label. A commission through affiliate links or discount codes counts too; switch on 'Paid Partnership' in Content Disclosure settings and, for India, also put the label in the post text.
Making the reader click through to understand the offer. The product, service or call to action must be clearly promoted without requiring users to click additional links.
Taking a health supplement, weight-loss, pharma, alcohol or political brief as an X paid partnership. Those categories are not eligible; offer another platform or format.
A UK own-brand post by someone with a commercial interest and no disclosure. That also needs one.
Assuming the toggle covers the law. Creators remain responsible for complying with all applicable laws and regulations.
applies_to: paid, gifted, affiliate and ambassador posts on X

rules.rule: A paid partnership includes products gifted by or on behalf of a brand, monetary or in-kind compensation, a commission from sales (for instance through affiliate links or discount codes), and brand-ambassador agreements.
Paid-partnership posts must have the 'Paid Partnership' disclosure on, set in Content Disclosure settings when posting; X then labels the post.

You are responsible for ensuring that any Paid Partnership you post complies with all applicable laws and regulations, and the product, service or call to action must be clearly promoted without requiring users to click on any additional links.

Not eligible for paid partnerships globally: adult products, alcohol, contraceptives, dating, drugs including CBD, 'Geo-political, political, social issues or crises for commercial purposes', health and wellness supplements, pharma and medicine, tobacco and vapes, weapons, and weight-loss products.
In Australia, the EU and the UK, financial products (loans, investments, crypto, buy-now-pay-later) and gambling are also not eligible.
UK: own-brand posts by someone with a commercial interest also need a disclosure.

checks: Is the post gifted, paid, affiliate, discount-code or ambassador content, and is the 'Paid Partnership' disclosure switched on?
Is the product category outside the not-eligible list (supplements, weight loss, pharma, alcohol, political and social-issue content and the rest)?
For Australia, EU or UK audiences, is it also outside financial products and gambling?
Does the post promote the product or call to action clearly within the post, without needing extra clicks to understand it?
For India, is the disclosure also written in the post itself (comp:asci_influencer)?
Is the post checked against the advertising law of the market it targets?
